extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Kantian philosophy; philosophers and graduate-level readers interested in epistemology and aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting the evaluative principles and conceptual distinctions Kant gives for the faculty of Judgement (its relation to Understanding and Reason, the distinction between determinant and reflective judgement, and the transcendental principle of purposiveness), as presented in the Preface and Introduction to the Critique of Judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of Philosophy into theoretical and practical
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy is divided into theoretical (Natural Philosophy) and practical (Moral Philosophy) parts, grounded on two kinds of concepts: natural concepts (which make theoretical cognition possible a priori) and the concept of freedom (which supplies the ground for practical legislation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The division is justified only if the concepts furnishing objects to the principles of rational cognition are specifically distinct; otherwise no genuine division exists. Theoretical concerns the legislation of Understanding through natural concepts; practical concerns legislation through the concept of freedom by Reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for a distinct part of Philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinct branch of Philosophy is constituted only if its principles rest on a principle not borrowed from the natural concept but on the supersensible (the concept of freedom), thereby giving morally practical precepts (laws) rather than technically practical precepts (precepts/corollaries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technically practical rules (arts, prudence, skill) that rest on natural concepts are corollaries of theoretical Philosophy and do not make a separate part. Only precepts based on the concept of freedom (supersensible) constitute the practical part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical (technically practical) vs moral (morally practical) rules
rubrics_metrics.description: If the concept determining the will is a natural concept, the principles are 'technically practical'; if the concept is the concept of freedom, they are 'morally practical'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technically practical rules are rules of skill and pertain to the possibility of things according to natural concepts (e.g., housekeeping, statesmanship). Morally practical rules are laws resting on the supersensible and are not mere precepts dependent on sensuous conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territory vs Realm (domicilium vs ditio) distinction for concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts referred to objects independently of the possibility of cognition have a field (territory) determined by the relation of their object to our cognitive faculty; the part of that field in which they are legislative is the 'realm' of those concepts and faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical concepts have territory (dwelling-place) in nature but no realm because they are not legislative a priori; realms belong to faculties/concepts that legislate a priori.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislation by Understanding versus Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation through natural concepts is carried on by the Understanding and is theoretical; legislation through the concept of freedom is by Reason and is practical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding and Reason exercise distinct a priori legislations in the same territory of experience without limiting each other in their legislation, even though they do so in the world of sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement as a mediating faculty with possible a priori principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgement is an intermediate faculty between Understanding and Reason (and between the faculty of knowledge and the faculty of desire via the feeling of pleasure and pain) and may contain in itself an a priori principle, though perhaps only subjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Judgement links understanding (knowledge) and reason (will/freedom) via the feeling of pleasure/pain, it is reasonable to suppose the Judgement might furnish a principle that effects transitions between these faculties—particularly relevant for aesthetic judgements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinant versus Reflective Judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinant Judgement subsumes the particular under a given universal (law given a priori by Understanding); Reflective Judgement, when only the particular is given, seeks the universal and must supply a principle from itself (cannot derive it from experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinant Judgement needs no law discovery; Reflective Judgement 'ascends from the particular in nature to the universal' and therefore requires a transcendental principle available only to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of the purposiveness of nature (formal purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle for reflective Judgement is that particular empirical laws, insofar as they are not fully determined by universal laws, must be considered as if an Understanding (not necessarily ours) furnished their unity—i.e., the purposiveness of nature in its manifoldness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purposiveness is a particular a priori concept originating solely in reflective Judgement: we represent nature 'as if' arranged according to purposes to make possible a systematic unity of empirical laws. This is a rule for our reflection, not an assertion about things in themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness of nature is distinct from practical purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The purposiveness employed by reflective Judgement (for thinking the unity of empirical laws) is quite different from practical purposiveness (as in human art or moral ends), though it is thought analogically to the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate the transcendental purposiveness that guides reflection about natural objects with teleological claims about actual purpose in nature or moral purposiveness; the former is a subjective principle for reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcendental vs Metaphysical principles distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: A transcendental principle represents a priori the universal condition under which alone things can be objects of our cognition; a metaphysical principle represents an a priori condition under which empirically given objects can be further determined a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the principle that bodies' changes must have a cause is transcendental; the claim that those changes must have an external cause is metaphysical. The purposiveness-of-nature principle is transcendental because it concerns possibility of empirical cognition generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness of nature as a transcendental principle requiring deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The purposiveness of nature for our cognitive faculties—manifest in maxims like 'nature takes the shortest way' or 'nature makes no leaps'—is a transcendental principle of Judgement and requires a Transcendental Deduction to ground it in sources of a priori cognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These maxims are not psychological descriptions of how we do judge, but prescriptive principles of how we ought to judge to secure unity of experience; they cannot be demonstrated purely from empirical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxims of Judgement (heuristic rules for reflecting on nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several maxims: 'Nature takes the shortest way' (lex parsimoniae); 'Nature makes no leaps' (lex continui in natura); 'Variety in empirical laws is unity under a few principles' (principia praeter necessitatem non sunt multiplicanda).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These function as transcendental heuristics directing reflective Judgement towards unified, lawlike explanation of empirical plurality; they are not empirical generalizations but regulative principles for systematic cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflective Judgement provides laws for the cognitive subject, not for nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The reflective Judgement gives a law only to itself (to guide our reflection and to secure the unity of empirical laws into a system), and does not prescribe laws to nature itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We must treat concepts like 'purpose' and 'purposiveness' as tools of reflective thought to systematize experience; they represent how we must proceed in judgment, not metaphysical features imposed on objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic Judgement as the principal puzzle for Judgement's principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetical judgements (concerning the Beautiful and the Sublime of Nature or of Art) present the main perplexity about whether Judgement contains an a priori principle that gives a rule a priori to the feeling of pleasure and pain, and whether such principles are constitutive or merely regulative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Critique of Judgement investigates whether Judgement's principles are constitutive or only regulative for feeling; the treatment is transcendental (concerned with possibility and bounds), not a guide to cultivating taste.
